verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Command the children of Israel, that they bring to you pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually.

Outside of the veil of the Testimony, in the Tent of Meeting, shall Aaron keep it in order from evening to morning before Yahweh continually: it shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.
He shall keep in order the lamps on the pure gold lamp stand before Yahweh continually.
“You shall take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes of it: two tenths of an ephah  shall be in one cake.
You shall set them in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table before Yahweh.
You shall put pure frankincense on each row, that it may be to the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant.
It shall be for Aaron and his sons; and they shall eat it in a holy place: for it is most holy to him of the offerings of Yahweh made by fire by a perpetual statute.”
The son of an Israelite woman, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the children of Israel; and the son of the Israelite woman and a man of Israel strove together in the camp.
The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name, and cursed; and they brought him to Moses. His mother’s name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.
They put him in custody, until Yahweh’s will should be declared to them.
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Bring out of the camp him who cursed; and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him.
You shall speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin.

He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
“‘He who strikes any man mortally shall surely be put to death.
He who strikes an animal mortally shall make it good, life for life.
If anyone injures his neighbor; as he has done, so shall it be done to him:
fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; as he has injured someone, so shall it be done to him.
He who kills an animal shall make it good; and he who kills a man shall be put to death.
You shall have one kind of law for the foreigner as well as the native-born; for I am Yahweh your God.’”
Moses spoke to the children of Israel; and they brought out him who had cursed out of the camp, and stoned him with stones. The children of Israel did as Yahweh commanded Moses.

footnotes.content: The Lord begins again with Moses, as He always does—not with demands, but with the voice of someone who loves to be known. This is how He speaks: 'I have something to show you, something to teach you.' The opening of His mouth is itself a gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pure olive oil, beaten—pressed under weight until it yields its light. The people are asked to bring it, a small act of obedience that keeps the light burning. I've learned that faithfulness often looks like showing up with what we have, again and again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lamp outside the veil, in the Tent of Meeting—this is the lampstand that stands in the holy place, and it must burn continually. Aaron tending it from evening to morning speaks to me of vigil, of faithfulness that doesn't sleep. The Lord loves a heart that keeps watch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ordering the lamps continually before the Lord—each one kept in its place, burning steadily. There's something about this image that speaks to the Spirit's work: He keeps us in order, tends us carefully, so that we might burn with His light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve cakes of fine flour, each one measured and deliberate. Twelve for the twelve tribes—each person seen, each family known. Even in provision there is order and care; the Lord numbers His people and provides for them by name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Set in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table—the Bread of the Presence, arranged for God to look upon. This bread represents the covenant and care between the Lord and His people. He sets before Himself what reminds Him of us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Frankincense on each row—the fragrant gift that rises as a memorial, a reminder before the Lord. It teaches me that even in the ordinary, we can offer something sweet. Our small obediences become fragrant before Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every Sabbath—again and again, the rhythm continues. An everlasting covenant spoken through the work of human hands. The Lord doesn't tire of His people; His commitment is renewed with every week, every offering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Most holy, for Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place—provision made sacred through obedience and place. The Lord remembers those who serve Him, and He feeds them with what is set apart. We belong to Him, and He tends to our needs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man of mixed heritage, whose father was Egyptian—he goes out among the Israel, where a quarrel breaks. Some belong on the edges, and edges are where tensions often erupt. But his place was known; he was a son of Israel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He blasphemes the Name—curses what is holy—and they bring him to Moses. His mother, Shelomith, is named; his tribe is named. Even in sin, the Lord knows who we are, where we come from, who bore us. We are never unknown to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He is held in custody while they wait for the Lord's will. Even in judgment, there is waiting—a pause for the Lord's voice to clarify what must be done. Hasty condemnation is not His way; His judgments come from wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again the Lord speaks to Moses, as He did at the start of the chapter. This second word is a word about consequences, about what follows when we curse the Name. God's speech can comfort, and it can also clarify what is true about holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bring him out of the camp—those who heard the curse lay their hands on his head, and all the congregation stones him. The community witnesses; the community enacts. The Name is a shared holiness, and the whole people are stewards of its protection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin. There is a weight to what we say, especially against the Holy One. Words are not wind; they carry consequence. This speaks to the seriousness with which the Lord holds us accountable for how we speak of Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who blasphemes Yahweh's name shall surely be put to death—the law is clear and without exception. The foreigner as well as the native-born face the same justice. This is a hard word, but it also teaches that the holiness of the Name is above all human distinction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who strikes any man mortally shall surely be put to death. Murder ends the life that was made in the image of God. To take a human life is to sin against the Creator; the penalty is absolute because the wrong is absolute.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who strikes an animal mortally shall make it good, life for life. Even beasts matter—they too are creation, and carelessness or cruelty toward them requires restoration. The Lord is concerned with all His works, not just those we think most important.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If anyone injures his neighbor, as he has done, so shall it be done to him. There is a principle of proportion in justice—not revenge, but balance. The Lord calls us to see that what we do to others is real, that it must be answered for, that equity matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth—this law appears again, and it speaks to the principle that injury demands correspondence, not excess. Even in ancient times, this protected the weak from disproportionate punishment. Justice must be measured.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who kills an animal shall make it good; and he who kills a man shall be put to death—there is a gradation in the law, reflecting the value of things. Human life, made in God's image, stands above all else. To preserve this teaching is to honor the Creator.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One kind of law for the foreigner as well as the native-born—the Lord insists on equality before His justice. No one's blood is worth more; no one's wrong is more forgivable based on where they come from. This is a high calling for His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: the Lord's word goes out, and His people do what He commands—not perfectly, not always willingly, but they align themselves with His will. In our own time, we too are invited into this alignment, to do as the Lord has spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
